claim: HiLITR converts protein colocalization into proteolytic release of a membrane-anchored transcription factor, which drives the expression of a chosen reporter gene.
source: HiLITR converts protein colocalization into proteolytic release of a membrane-anchored transcription factor, which drives the expression of a chosen reporter gene.
evidence: This is a direct description of the HiLITR mechanism from the abstract.

claim: Using HiLITR in combination with FACS-based CRISPRi screening in human cell lines, genes that influence the trafficking of mitochondrial and ER tail-anchored proteins were identified.
source: Using HiLITR in combination with FACS-based CRISPRi screening in human cell lines, we identified genes that influence the trafficking of mitochondrial and ER tail-anchored proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Loss of the SUMO E1 component SAE1 results in mislocalization and destabilization of many mitochondrial tail-anchored proteins.
source: We show that loss of the SUMO E1 component SAE1 results in mislocalization and destabilization of many mitochondrial tail-anchored proteins.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: EMC10 has a distinct regulatory role in the ER membrane complex, opposing the transmembrane-domain insertion activity of the complex.
source: We also demonstrate a distinct regulatory role for EMC10 in the ER membrane complex, opposing the transmembrane-domain insertion activity of the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: CRISPR-based knockout screens have identified essential human genes.
source: For example, CRISPR-based knockout screens have identified essential human genes (Hart et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CRISPR-based knockout screens have discovered factors that confer drug or toxin resistance.
source: For example, CRISPR-based knockout screens have identified essential human genes (Hart et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), discovered factors that confer drug or toxin resistance (Wang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CRISPR-based knockout screens have dissected signaling and regulatory networks.
source: For example, CRISPR-based knockout screens have identified essential human genes (Hart et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015), discovered factors that confer drug or toxin resistance (Wang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), and dissected signaling and regulatory networks (Klann et al., 2017; Parnas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pooled screens simplify the handling of large libraries with >10^5 unique elements.
source: Pooled screens simplify the handling of large libraries with >105 unique elements (Kampmann et al., 2015; Morgens et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pooled screens require that the cellular function of interest be coupled to a simple readout, such as cell proliferation or fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: Pooled screens simplify the handling of large libraries with >105 unique elements (Kampmann et al., 2015; Morgens et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015), but require that the cellular function of interest be coupled to a simple readout, such as cell proliferation (Han et al., 2020; Kory et al., 2018) or fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS; DeJesus et al., 2016; Potting et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arrayed screens are well-suited to complex readouts, such as high-content or time-lapse microscopy.
source: Arrayed screens, on the other hand, are well-suited to complex readouts, such as high-content or time-lapse microscopy, and have been used to discover factors that regulate cell division (Neumann et al., 2010), endocytosis (Liberali et al., 2014), and membrane protein trafficking (Hansen et al., 2018; Krumpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arrayed screens have been used to discover factors that regulate cell division.
source: Arrayed screens, on the other hand, are well-suited to complex readouts, such as high-content or time-lapse microscopy, and have been used to discover factors that regulate cell division (Neumann et al., 2010), endocytosis (Liberali et al., 2014), and membrane protein trafficking (Hansen et al., 2018; Krumpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arrayed screens have been used to discover factors that regulate endocytosis.
source: Arrayed screens, on the other hand, are well-suited to complex readouts, such as high-content or time-lapse microscopy, and have been used to discover factors that regulate cell division (Neumann et al., 2010), endocytosis (Liberali et al., 2014), and membrane protein trafficking (Hansen et al., 2018; Krumpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Arrayed screens have been used to discover factors that regulate membrane protein trafficking.
source: Arrayed screens, on the other hand, are well-suited to complex readouts, such as high-content or time-lapse microscopy, and have been used to discover factors that regulate cell division (Neumann et al., 2010), endocytosis (Liberali et al., 2014), and membrane protein trafficking (Hansen et al., 2018; Krumpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compared to pooled screens, arrayed screens are usually noisier, limited to smaller libraries (10^3–10^4), and are more technically difficult and time-consuming to implement.
source: However, compared to pooled screens, arrayed screens are usually noisier, limited to smaller libraries (103–104), and are more technically difficult and time-consuming to implement, requiring specialized instrumentation not available to all laboratories.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of arrayed screens based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: HiLITR is a molecular tool that converts protein localization or mislocalization into simple expression of a fluorescent protein.
source: Here we report HiLITR (High-throughput Localization Indicator with Transcriptional Readout), a molecular tool that converts protein localization or mislocalization into simple expression of a fluorescent protein.
evidence: This is a direct description of HiLITR from the introduction.

claim: Knockdown of the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E1 ligase component SAE1 selectively destabilizes and increases the mislocalization of many mitochondrial tail-anchored (TA) proteins.
source: We found that knockdown of the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E1 ligase component SAE1 selectively destabilizes and increases the mislocalization of many mitochondrial tail-anchored (TA) proteins.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Knockdown of the EMC10 subunit of the ER membrane complex (EMC) increases insertion of specific TA proteins into the ERM, in opposition to the function of other EMC components.
source: Additionally, we found that knockdown of the EMC10 subunit of the ER membrane complex (EMC) increases insertion of specific TA proteins into the ERM, in opposition to the function of other EMC components.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: When the HiLITR protease and TF are colocalized to the same organelle, proximity-dependent proteolysis of a protease cleavage sequence (TEVcs) in the TF's membrane anchor releases the TF, which can translocate to the nucleus and drive expression of a chosen reporter gene.
source: If the protease and TF are colocalized to the same organelle (e.g., the mitochondrial membrane in Figure 1A), then proximity-dependent proteolysis of a protease cleavage sequence (TEVcs) in the TF's membrane anchor releases the TF, which can translocate to the nucleus and drive expression of a chosen reporter gene.
evidence: This is a description of the HiLITR mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: If the HiLITR protease and TF are not colocalized, then TF cleavage and reporter gene expression will not occur.
source: If the protease and TF are not colocalized, then TF cleavage and reporter gene expression will not occur.
evidence: This is a description of the HiLITR mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The LOV domain sterically blocks protease cleavage in the dark, but changes conformation to provide access under blue light illumination.
source: The LOV domain sterically blocks protease cleavage in the dark, but changes conformation to provide access under blue light illumination.
evidence: This is a description of the LOV domain function in HiLITR.

claim: HiLITR acts as an AND gate, requiring both protease/TF colocalization and blue light to turn on.
source: HiLITR therefore acts as an AND gate, requiring both protease/TF colocalization and blue light to turn on.
evidence: This is a description of the HiLITR mechanism.

claim: The two-gate design of HiLITR improves the dynamic range, temporal precision, and tunability compared to a one-gate design.
source: This two-gate design improves the dynamic range, temporal precision, and tunability compared to a one-gate design (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Transient transfection of HiLITR components produced high background signal.
source: Transient transfection produced high background signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B)
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Stable integration of HiLITR components alleviated the high background signal observed with transient transfection.
source: Transient transfection produced high background signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), which was alleviated by stable integration (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Replacing TEV protease with the approximately fivefold more catalytically efficient 'ultraTEV' (S153N) improved HiLITR specificity.
source: We improved specificity by replacing TEV protease with the approximately fivefold more catalytically efficient 'ultraTEV' (S153N) (Sanchez and Ting, 2020) and the eLOV domain with the tighter-dark state hLOV (Kim et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F, supported by citations.

claim: Replacing the eLOV domain with the tighter-dark state hLOV improved HiLITR specificity.
source: We improved specificity by replacing TEV protease with the approximately fivefold more catalytically efficient 'ultraTEV' (S153N) (Sanchez and Ting, 2020) and the eLOV domain with the tighter-dark state hLOV (Kim et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F, supported by citations.

claim: Replacement of the Gal4 TF with a more active Gal4-VP64 fusion improved HiLITR signal.
source: Replacement of the Gal4 TF with a more active Gal4-VP64 fusion also improved signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and H).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and H.

claim: Compared to the previous protein interaction-detecting tool SPARK, HiLITR detects colocalized proteins with superior sensitivity and specificity.
source: Compared to our previous protein interaction-detecting tool SPARK (Kim et al., 2017), HiLITR detects colocalized proteins with superior sensitivity and specificity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I–K, supported by a citation.

claim: In K562 cells, ERM-TF was clearly activated by ERM protease, but not by OMM protease or cytosolic protease.
source: By FACS in K562 cells (Figure 1D), we observed clear activation of ERM-TF by ERM protease, but not by OMM protease or cytosolic protease.
evidence: This is an observation from the FACS experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In K562 cells, OMM-TF was clearly activated by OMM protease but not by ERM protease or cytosolic protease.
source: We also saw clear activation of OMM-TF by OMM protease but not by ERM protease or cytosolic protease.
evidence: This is an observation from the FACS experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The absence of cross-reactivity between OMM-TF and ERM protease is striking given that mitochondria and ER form contacts in mammalian cells.
source: The absence of cross-reactivity is striking given that mitochondria and ER form contacts in mammalian cells (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, with a citation to support the existence of ER-mitochondria contacts.

claim: The fraction of HiLITR TF localized to ER-mitochondria contact sites is very small compared to the total amount of TF on the OMM or ERM surface, such that the contribution of ER-mitochondria contacts to HiLITR activation is insignificant.
source: Perhaps the fraction of HiLITR TF localized to these contact sites is very small compared to the total amount of TF on the OMM or ERM surface, such that the contribution of ER-mitochondria contacts to HiLITR activation is insignificant.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of cross-reactivity.

claim: HiLITR constructs localized to the peroxisomal membrane gave expected patterns of activation.
source: As an additional test of specificity, we designed HiLITR constructs localized to the peroxisomal membrane, which also gave expected patterns of activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F and G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F and G.

claim: qPCR analysis showed >300-fold enrichment of cells with colocalized HiLITR components from cells with non-colocalized HiLITR components in a single round of FACS.
source: qPCR analysis showed >300-fold enrichment in a single round of FACS (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Several distinct pathways orchestrate the co-translational or post-translational insertion of proteins at the ERM.
source: Several distinct pathways orchestrate the co-translational or post-translational insertion of these proteins at the ERM (Shao and Hegde, 2011) and at the OMM (Hansen and Herrmann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several distinct pathways orchestrate the co-translational or post-translational insertion of proteins at the OMM.
source: Several distinct pathways orchestrate the co-translational or post-translational insertion of these proteins at the ERM (Shao and Hegde, 2011) and at the OMM (Hansen and Herrmann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies have revealed a striking interplay between ER and mitochondrial membrane targeting pathways.
source: Recent studies have also revealed a striking interplay between ER and mitochondrial membrane targeting pathways (Costa et al., 2018; Gamerdinger et al., 2015; Mårtensson et al., 2019), such as the ER-SURF pathway, in which some OMM proteins are harbored on the ERM when mitochondrial import is impaired (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ER-SURF pathway is a pathway in which some OMM proteins are harbored on the ERM when mitochondrial import is impaired.
source: Recent studies have also revealed a striking interplay between ER and mitochondrial membrane targeting pathways (Costa et al., 2018; Gamerdinger et al., 2015; Mårtensson et al., 2019), such as the ER-SURF pathway, in which some OMM proteins are harbored on the ERM when mitochondrial import is impaired (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanisms by which tail-anchored mitochondrial proteins are delivered and inserted into the OMM are unclear.
source: For example, the mechanisms by which tail-anchored mitochondrial proteins are delivered and inserted into the OMM are unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: There are about 40 human mitochondrial TA proteins.
source: There are about 40 human mitochondrial TA proteins, including the apoptosis regulators BAX and BCL2 (Wolter et al., 1997) and mitochondrial fission proteins FIS1 (Yoon et al., 2003) and MFF (Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the number of mitochondrial TA proteins, supported by citations.

claim: BAX and BCL2 are apoptosis regulators.
source: There are about 40 human mitochondrial TA proteins, including the apoptosis regulators BAX and BCL2 (Wolter et al., 1997) and mitochondrial fission proteins FIS1 (Yoon et al., 2003) and MFF (Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FIS1 and MFF are mitochondrial fission proteins.
source: There are about 40 human mitochondrial TA proteins, including the apoptosis regulators BAX and BCL2 (Wolter et al., 1997) and mitochondrial fission proteins FIS1 (Yoon et al., 2003) and MFF (Gandre-Babbe and van der Bliek, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The targeting of TA proteins presents a unique challenge because their hydrophobic transmembrane domains are translated last and must be handed off from the ribosome to appropriate chaperones or lipids before aggregation or misfolding can occur.
source: The targeting of TA proteins presents a unique challenge because their hydrophobic transmembrane domains are translated last and must be handed off from the ribosome to appropriate chaperones or lipids before aggregation or misfolding can occur.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of TA protein targeting based on established knowledge.

claim: The GET/transmembrane recognition complex (TRC) pathway, responsible for targeting of endomembrane system TA proteins to the ER, is not required for targeting of mitochondrial TA proteins.
source: It is known that the GET/transmembrane recognition complex (TRC) pathway, responsible for targeting of endomembrane system TA proteins to the ER, is not required for targeting of mitochondrial TA proteins (Borgese et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In yeast, the HSP70 protein Sti1 (human STIP1) and Pex19 may play a role in mitochondrial TA protein targeting.
source: In yeast, the HSP70 protein Sti1 (human STIP1) and Pex19 may play a role in mitochondrial TA protein targeting (Cichocki et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In vitro experiments with proteolytically shaved mitochondria show that unassisted or minimally assisted insertion of mitochondrial TA proteins may be possible.
source: but in vitro experiments with proteolytically shaved mitochondria show that unassisted or minimally assisted insertion may also be possible (Kemper et al., 2008; Setoguchi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the TA screen, impaired mitochondrial localization of a TA protease would reduce the release of a SA mitochondrial TF, diminishing HiLITR activation.
source: In the most direct approach, impaired mitochondrial localization of a TA protease would reduce the release of a SA mitochondrial TF, diminishing HiLITR activation ('TA screen'; Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the TA screen design, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: The 'loss of signal' design of the TA screen may enrich false-positive genes whose knockdown either nonspecifically disrupts HiLITR component expression or impairs trafficking of the SA TF, rather than the protease.
source: However, this 'loss of signal' design may enrich false-positive genes whose knockdown either nonspecifically disrupts HiLITR component expression (e.g., ribosomal proteins) or impairs trafficking of the SA TF, rather than the protease.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential limitations of the TA screen design.

claim: Comparison of TA and SA screen results should eliminate most false positives and identify factors that selectively influence the targeting of mitochondrial TA over SA proteins.
source: Comparison of TA and SA screen results should eliminate most false positives and identify factors that selectively influence the targeting of mitochondrial TA over SA proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the SA screen design.

claim: Disrupted or nontargeted mitochondrial TA protease may reroute to the ERM (and subsequently to other organelles connected to the ER such as the Golgi).
source: For our third HiLITR configuration, we designed a 'gain of signal' screen based on the hypothesis that disrupted or nontargeted mitochondrial TA protease may reroute to the ERM (and subsequently to other organelles connected to the ER such as the Golgi).
evidence: This is a hypothesis underlying the ER screen design.

claim: The ER screen might help to identify factors that regulate the targeting of native ERM proteins.
source: Given the partial ER localization of this mTA* protease, we anticipated that our ER screen might also help to identify factors that regulate the targeting of native ERM proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the potential utility of the ER screen.

claim: A whole-genome 'TA screen' was performed with HiLITR components shown in Figure 2C.
source: To first narrow down our list of candidate genes, we performed a whole-genome 'TA screen' with the HiLITR components shown in Figure 2C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Human K562 cells expressing HiLITR and the CRISPRi repressor dCas9-BFP-KRAB were transduced with a library of sgRNAs targeting 20,000 genes, at 5 guides/gene, with 1,900 nontargeting controls.
source: Human K562 cells expressing HiLITR and the CRISPRi repressor dCas9-BFP-KRAB were transduced with a library of sgRNAs targeting 20,000 genes, at 5 guides/gene, with 1,900 nontargeting controls.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Next-generation sequencing of sgRNA abundance in the collected populations indicated enrichment of genes related to protein folding, membrane trafficking, and proteasome function in the low mCherry cell population.
source: Next-generation sequencing of sgRNA abundance in the collected populations indicated enrichment of genes related to protein folding, membrane trafficking, and proteasome function in the low mCherry cell population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The whole-genome screen enriched a number of gene expression-related false positives, including ribosome subunits, mediator complex subunits, and mRNA binding proteins.
source: As expected, we also enriched a number of gene expression-related false positives, including ribosome subunits, mediator complex subunits, and mRNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from the sequencing data.

claim: An sgRNA sublibrary was designed for simultaneous screening in the three HiLITR configurations (TA screen, SA screen, and ER screen).
source: Using these results, we designed an sgRNA sublibrary (Supplementary file 2) for simultaneous screening in the three HiLITR configurations (TA screen, SA screen, and ER screen).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The sgRNA sublibrary contained 2,930 sgRNAs targeting 586 genes (5 guides/gene) plus 500 nontargeting controls.
source: In total, we transduced our three clonal HiLITR K562 cell lines with 2,930 sgRNAs targeting 586 genes (5 guides/gene) plus 500 nontargeting controls.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Two biological replicates were performed for each HiLITR configuration.
source: Two biological replicates were performed for each HiLITR configuration.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The screens were performed at 2,000–10,000× coverage in order to detect subtle or partial effects.
source: The screens were performed as shown in Figure 2B, with infection, passaging, and sorting carried out at 2,000–10,000× coverage – a higher level than standard – in order to detect subtle or partial effects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Sequencing data were analyzed by CasTLE, which assigns to each gene an effect size and an associated CasTLE score (a measure of significance, signed for effect direction).
source: Sequencing data were analyzed by CasTLE (Morgens et al., 2016), which assigns to each gene an effect size and an associated CasTLE score (a measure of significance, signed for effect direction).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: CasTLE scores in the TA and SA screens were largely concordant, reflecting the similarity between the two configurations (R2 = 0.69).
source: CasTLE scores in the TA and SA screens were largely concordant, reflecting the similarity between the two configurations (R2 = 0.69, compared to R2 = 0.28 for TA vs. ER screens and 0.37 for SA vs. ER screens).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Out of 586 genes, sgRNAs against 270 of them impacted HiLITR turn-on significantly (at 10% false discovery rate [FDR]) in at least one screen.
source: Out of 586 genes, sgRNAs against 270 of them impacted HiLITR turn-on significantly (at 10% false discovery rate [FDR]) in at least one screen (186 genes in 2+ screens).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Of the 50 most significant genes from the whole-genome screen that were included in the three-screen sublibrary, 47 were significant in the TA screen at 10% FDR, indicating good reproducibility.
source: The TA screen and whole-genome screens used the same HiLITR configuration, and of the 50 most significant genes from the whole-genome screen that were included in the three-screen sublibrary, 47 were significant in the TA screen at 10% FDR, indicating good reproducibility.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The TRC pathway is the first pathway discovered for the targeting of ER-destined TA proteins and is well-characterized.
source: The TRC pathway (Schuldiner et al., 2008; Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007), which handles the membrane insertion of ER TA proteins, also mishandles overexpressed mitochondrial TA proteins (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The TRC pathway handles the membrane insertion of ER TA proteins.
source: The TRC pathway (Schuldiner et al., 2008; Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007), which handles the membrane insertion of ER TA proteins, also mishandles overexpressed mitochondrial TA proteins (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The TRC pathway mishandles overexpressed mitochondrial TA proteins.
source: The TRC pathway (Schuldiner et al., 2008; Stefanovic and Hegde, 2007), which handles the membrane insertion of ER TA proteins, also mishandles overexpressed mitochondrial TA proteins (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown of the TRC pathway chaperones SGTA and TRC40 significantly altered HiLITR activation in the TA and ER screens, but not the SA screen.
source: Consistent with this activity, knockdown of the TRC pathway chaperones SGTA and TRC40 significantly altered HiLITR activation in the TA and ER screens, but not the SA screen (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Other TRC pathway components also altered HiLITR activation in the TA and ER screens.
source: Other TRC pathway components also altered HiLITR activation in the TA and ER screens (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EMC handles insertion of a subset of TA proteins at the ERM.
source: The EMC, similar to the TRC pathway, handles insertion of a subset of TA proteins at the ERM (Guna et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Among nine EMC subunits tested, eight significantly altered HiLITR activation uniquely in the ER screen.
source: Among nine subunits tested, eight significantly altered HiLITR activation uniquely in the ER screen (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SAE1 is an essential protein and a member of the SAE complex (along with SAE2/UBA2), which acts as the sole SUMO E1 ligase in mammalian cells.
source: SAE1 is an essential protein and a member of the SAE complex (along with SAE2/UBA2), which acts as the sole SUMO E1 ligase in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a statement about SAE1 based on established knowledge.

claim: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can alter protein subcellular localization.
source: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can alter protein subcellular localization (Martin et al., 2007; Matunis et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can regulate protein stability.
source: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can alter protein subcellular localization (Martin et al., 2007; Matunis et al., 1996), regulate protein stability (Desterro et al., 1998; Krumova et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can promote cellular stress response.
source: Modification of target proteins with the small protein tag SUMO can alter protein subcellular localization (Martin et al., 2007; Matunis et al., 1996), regulate protein stability (Desterro et al., 1998; Krumova et al., 2011), and promote cellular stress response (Golebiowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several important mitochondrial proteins are SUMOylation targets, including Parkin and Drp1.
source: Several important mitochondrial proteins are SUMOylation targets, including Parkin (Um and Chung, 2006) and Drp1 (Prudent et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several chaperones implicated in the handling of TA proteins, including the ubiquilins and STIP1, are SUMOylated.
source: Intriguingly, several chaperones implicated in the handling of TA proteins, including the ubiquilins (Itakura et al., 2016) and STIP1, are also SUMOylated (Hendriks et al., 2018; Soares et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several genes involved in mitosis and cytoskeletal functions were among the hits with low TA score and mid-to-high SA score, including BORA, CCNK, REEP4, MKI67IP, and SKA1.
source: Several genes involved in mitosis and cytoskeletal functions were among the hits with low TA score and mid-to-high SA score, including BORA, CCNK, REEP4, MKI67IP, and SKA1, (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ATP6V1A, a subunit of the vacuolar ATPase, was among the hits with low TA score and high ER score.
source: The quadrant with low TA score and high ER score (Figure 3D) contained only a few hits, one of which was ATP6V1A, a subunit of the vacuolar ATPase, which has an important role in vesicle trafficking (Dettmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an observation from the screen data shown in Figure 3D, supported by a citation.

claim: The vacuolar ATPase has an important role in vesicle trafficking.
source: The quadrant with low TA score and high ER score (Figure 3D) contained only a few hits, one of which was ATP6V1A, a subunit of the vacuolar ATPase, which has an important role in vesicle trafficking (Dettmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Four hits (SAE1, CCNK, SKA1, and ATP6V1A) were validated by individual sgRNA experiments.
source: We selected SAE1 (Figure 4) and seven additional hits from Figure 3D and E for validation. Four of these hits (SAE1, CCNK, SKA1, and ATP6V1A) were validated (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This is an observation from the validation experiments shown in Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Knockdown of SKA1 or ATP6V1A increased the fraction of GFP-mTA* protease mislocalized to the Golgi.
source: and we found by imaging that knockdown of SKA1 or ATP6V1A increased the fraction of GFP-mTA* protease mislocalized to the Golgi (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and 2G; a consequence of anterograde trafficking after mistargeting to the ER).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and 2G.

claim: Validation with individual sgRNAs against SAE1 in HiLITR cell lines recapitulated the results of the CRISPRi screens.
source: Validation with individual sgRNAs against SAE1 in HiLITR cell lines recapitulated the results of the CRISPRi screens (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the validation experiments shown in Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: SAE1 knockdown specifically reduced the abundance of GFP-tagged mitochondrial TA protease, but not GFP-tagged mitochondrial SA protease.
